utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I wish everyone a very good -- a very happy and healthy new year. The Chamber has a number of pending matters it wishes to deal with orally before starting with the testimony of the witnesses scheduled for today. The Chamber would first note that the Tribunal shall be closed for operations on the 24th and 25th of March due to the holding of the Nuclear Security Summit at the World Forum. While the Chamber expects the Defence case to be completed by then, in the event that it is not, any hearing scheduled for these two days would have to be rescheduled. Next, On the 14th of January, 2014, the Chamber was notified of an e-mail of the same day sent to its legal staff by the accused's legal advisor communicating a request from Predrag Banovic, a prospective witness to be called by the Defence at the end of January, for the assignment of counsel for the purposes of his testimony at the Tribunal. The Prosecution indicated via e-mail of the same day that it did not wish to respond. The Chamber has considered Article 5 of the directive on the assignment of counsel, which provides for the assignment of counsel to three categories of individuals: i.e., suspects, accused persons, and any persons detained under the authority of the Tribunal. Banovic was released in 2008 and is therefore no longer covered by Article 5 of the directive. The Chamber sees no exceptional circumstances warranting that the Chamber order the Registrar to assign counsel to Banovic for the purpose of his testimony in these proceedings. The Chamber now turns to the accused's motion for advance notice of questions to be posed to Colonel Ljubisa Beara filed on the 23rd of December, 2013 wherein the accused requests that the Chamber order the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 54 and 73, to provide advance written notice of the questions it intends to put to Ljubisa Beara during its cross-examination scheduled for 22nd January of 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The accused submits that the given Bera's special circumstances as an appellant in Tribunal proceedings, who is being subpoenaed to testify in this case, this would serve to ensure that his rights are safe-guarded. The Prosecution responded on the 7th of January, 2014, opposing the motion. The Prosecution contends that the motion amounts to a subversion of the truth-seeking process, has no basis in the Rules, and would be inconsistent with the practice applied in this trial. During cross-examination, Bera will be assisted by counsel who is fully acquainted of the charges against Beara and his case on appeal. As he did during examination-in-chief, counsel for Beara will be in a position to object if it deems that a particular question put to Beara may incriminate him. As it did on direct, the Chamber will consider that objection and render its ruling. The Chamber, therefore, sees no reason to grant the motion and request that the Prosecution submit its questions in advance of testimony. The Chamber also recalls that now that Beara's testimony has started and he has taken the oath, he may no longer discuss the contents of his testimony with anyone. He would therefore not be in position to consult his counsel on the substance of the questions communicated by the Prosecution which would consequently not serve the purpose put forth by the accused. The motion is therefore denied. The Chamber will now turn to the accused's request for order to commander of the UN Detention Unit filed on the 8th of January, 2014, in which the accused requests that the Chamber direct the UNDU commander to provide a report on the behaviour of the accused since his arrival at the UNDU at 2008. The UNDU commander has previously informed the accused that he would not provide such a report unless ordered by the Chamber. On the 9th of January, 2014, the Prosecution indicated via e-mail that it did not wish to respond to the request. Given that the accused intends to use this report for the purpose of sentencing submissions, the Chamber hereby grants the request and orders that the UNDU commander provide the accused with a report of his behaviour since his arrival at the UNDU in 2008 as soon as practicable, and in any event, by no later than 28th of February, 2014. Finally, the Chamber would like to receive expedited responses to motions related to Mladic's testimony in this case. First, both the accused and the Prosecution should respond to Mladic's urgent motion for reconsideration of decisions -- decision on motion for certification to appeal filed on the 14th of January, 2014, before Friday, 17th January, close of business. And, second, the accused should respond to the urgent Prosecution motion for reconsideration of decision on Mladic request for certification to appeal subpoena decision filed on the 15th of January 2014, also no later than Friday, 17 January, close of business. That said, unless there's anything further, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we bring in the witness, I can just advise the Chamber that this morning we did file our responses to those two motions concerning General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Nikolic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any questions from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, incriminate means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. And I would like to wish everyone a happy new year, and season's greetings.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us pause between my questions and your answers so that we would have a proper transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 1D09650.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, take a look on the left-hand side of the screen. Can you see that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be displayed with Mr. Nikolic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This statement, does it faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team, exactly as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this Rule -- this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Although the Prosecution does note that this statement contains multiple leading questions; for example, questions 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, and 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Vinko Nikolic's statement. [In English] Vinko Nikolic lived in Sanski Most when the war broke out in BH. For a time he was a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff. Before the beginning of the war, the Muslims were arming themselves especially in those villages where they formed a majority of the population. The first incident in Sanski Most was the killing of a Serb, Predrag Dobrijevic, a member of the 6th Sana Brigade. The next incident was at the check-point set up by Muslim residents of the village of Trnova. The Muslim extremists stopped two civilian policemen who were on regular patrol and disarmed them. The crisis in Sanski Most arose primarily because of the breakup of the former SFRY. After the breakup of the SFRY and the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, some of the young, demobilised soldiers and columns of soldiers, the JNA vehicles passed through the municipality of Sanski Most. They did not provoke anyone, as they passed through without weapons, but these innocent soldiers were still called Chetnik murders and other insulting names. In order to preserve the peace and avert the conflict, the representatives of the Serbian authorities offered a division of the municipality of Sanski Most into two parts, two municipalities. The Muslims did not accept the offer and instead opted for the conflict and war. The Serbian political leadership and the leadership of the Sanski Most public security station offered the all Muslim and Croatian professional policemen a chance to remain in the police force. Only one policeman of Croatian ethnicity accepted while all the others tried to set up a Muslim police station in the Sanski Most municipality, occupying the Sanski Most municipality building. Since they ignored the ultimatum to leave the building and surrender their weapons, the Serbian police disarmed them and liberated the building. Since the Muslim side did not accept the proposal for a peaceful solution to the crisis and clearly wanted complete control over Sanski Most, there were major incidents that night caused by individuals and groups. These people used this period of chaos for their own ends. On 25th of March 1992, the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most was proclaimed, but all citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, were allowed to remain in their jobs if they respected the constitution of the Republika Srpska BH. From 1992 to 1995, more than 8.000 Muslims continued to live in Sanski Most municipality. After the first incidents and as the situation deteriorated, most of the Muslim population, probably on the instruction of their own political party, moved out their families along before -- before March 1992. Before the fighting started, some of the Muslim families sent their children to places in BH which had Muslim majority, or to Croatia or Slovenia. When people decided voluntarily to leave, the Red Cross and the Civilian Protection had an obligation to help them to do that. They secured the convoys and tried to ensure that there were no incidents. The Sanski Most Crisis Staff issued an order that all property was to be looked after and temporarily allocated as needed to the Serbian refugees. Anyone who had broken the law, possessed weapons, threatened the safety of citizens and did not respect the Republika Srpska constitution had no right to work in the municipality. These people had to answer for their actions and their proceedings, and taking of statements was mainly done by members of the civilian and military police. The investigation centres were used to question them. The officials of the military and civilian police forces performed their duties in the best possible professional manner. No one was allowed to mistreat or beat the people from whom the statements were taken. On one occasion, a policeman was caught mistreating a Muslim and immediately removed from the investigation duty. The political leadership tried to protect all civilians of Sanski Most who had not broken the constitution or the laws. The civilian authorities, the civilian police and the army did not plan, instigate, or order the permanent removal of the Bosnian Muslims from the area, as it is shown by the large number of -- who continued to live in Sanski Most right up until 1995. And that is the summary of statement. And at that moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing. That is, through your written statement. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in your statement, you explain that you were for a time a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff and you were also a member of the SOS, or the Serbian Defence Forces. I'd just like to clarify various roles. So it's true, isn't it, that you were a member of the Crisis Staff from its creation on the 14th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3329.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nikolic, while this is coming up this is the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula, who you will recall was the Crisis Staff president. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And do you recall that on the 14th of April, an extended session of the Municipal Board of the SDS was held in the Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just look at notes of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see page 11 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This may refresh your recollection. And I'm interested in the section which states: "Course of action in taking over power and establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most?" And a little further down it says: "14 April 1992 a session of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party with increased attendance was held and the following decided..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we look at item 4 it states: "The Crisis Staff, consisting of the following members, shall be in charge of all actions?" And the last name in this list of members is Zvonko Nikolic. Now that should be a reference to you Vinko Nikolic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm Vinko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This reference -- just to be clear, this reference in Mr. Rasula's diary relates to you, Vinko Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting, you were appointed as the SOS representative on the Crisis Staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then at a later meeting, on the 30th of May, 1992, you were formally appointed a Crisis Staff member, and you were the member of the Crisis Staff in charge of vehicles. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then as of 18th of June, you were no longer a permanent member of the Crisis Staff but, rather, you were appointed a commissioner for transport. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3666.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nikolic, you'll see that these are the conclusions from the Crisis Staff meeting of 18th of June, and it states that the -- it lists the permanent members of the Crisis Staff, beginning with Mladen Lukic, and then it lists the commissioners of the Crisis Staff. And at number 3, you'll see your name, Vinko Nikolic, commission for transport. So does that refresh your recollection? You were appointed the commissioner for transport?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. Because sometime around the 1st of June, I belonged to the 6th Sana Brigade, and I was on the front line that entire month, together with other SOS members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll come back to your activities during that period. But just as a preliminary, the SOS worked together with the Sanski Most Crisis Staff. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And prior to its subordination to the VRS, the SOS acted on Crisis Staff instructions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, the SOS worked together with the Crisis Staff in the implementation of republic level and ARK level instructions from the SDS. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And could we please see P3397.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this is a report on the work and the activities of the SOS acting as intervention platoon within the 6th Krajina Brigade between the 1st of May and the 6th of September, 1992. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I've not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we go to the signature page, please, of this document. It's the last page in both versions. And if we could focus on the signatures in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you recognise these signatures?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this document was issued by the SOS, not by the 6th Sana Brigade. It is not a report by the 6th Sana Brigade but, rather, by the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And can you -- can you read out the signatures of this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dusan Savic, who was the commander of the SOS, that's one signature; my signature; and also Cankovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at this stage, I'm interested in a passage at page 3 of the document in both the B/C/S and the English versions. And it's the third paragraph down in the English and at the very bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and it states: "Remember the meeting we had on the premises of the Serbian Orthodox church where we particularly warned about the slow implementation of the conclusions reached by the Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS and the Bosnian Krajina..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Nikolic, is: This is an example of the SDS or, excuse me, the SOS encouraging the implementation of the conclusions reached by the republic level SDS and the ARK level SDS, as you've previously acknowledged?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the events of the 19th of April and their aftermath. In your response to question 9, you discuss how the Serbian police force and the TO liberated the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly building and in your response to question 29 you state that the 6th Krajina Brigade was not involved until the early hours of the morning. You will agree, will you, Mr. Nikolic, that this was a significant military operation involving a large show of strength between or -- or by the Serb TO, the SOS, and the JNA in and around Sanski Most town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. The JNA did not participate in the action to liberate the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: However, the JNA assisted you in the immediate aftermath of that -- of that operation.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA arrived and took over the facility and secured it. They did everything to prevent chaos that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, you said -- and that reflects what you said in your statement in your answer to your question 15 where you say that General Talic visited Sanski Most to see for himself the security situation and to try and prevent conflict and to save all of Sanski Most citizens. Now, General Talic visited Sanski Most the day after the take-over on the 20th of April, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And he met with SDA and HDZ representatives. Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nikolic, there's evidence before the Trial Chamber that at that meeting, General Talic told the Muslims not to ask for help or otherwise they would have another Kupres, Bosanski Brod or Vukovar. Now, this kind of threat to the Muslims and the Croats doesn't suggest a desire on General Talic's part to protect all the citizens of Sanski Most, does it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what General Talic said to the Muslims, but I know that an order was issued to the effect that the situation had to be at peace at all costs in order to avoid any further skirmishes or fire being opened, or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, we'll come on to the skirmishes, but during this -- well, you state in question 10 that after the liberation of the municipality building, this period of chaos ensued in which roads were blocked and telephone lines were down. Do you agree, however, that the Sanski Most authorities continued to be in contact with the ARK authorities and the republic level authorities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you also state that in this period of chaos there was looting, burning of houses, and other chaos before the authorities got the situation under control. Now, we'll come back to the burning of houses and the destruction of buildings. But it's true, isn't it, that stealing was -- or looting, rather, was not the only stealing of goods that was taking place, but there were also check-points set up by the military police and the SOS confiscated goods and vehicles at these check-point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The military police did set up check-points but the SOS could not confiscate anything. We didn't have that much power.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you personally were responsible for the appropriation of trucks and other vehicles from a company called Agrokomerc, which was headquartered in the Muslim controlled area of Velika Kladusa; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. Those trucks were stopped by the Territorial Defence on the highway that by-passed Sanski Most. An order from the Crisis Staff was to place those trucks in a safe place which is why I received that order, and we placed the trucks at the stadium of the Podumic [phoen] football team, only a fence separated from the police station. That's where they were safe, and that's how we prevented the stealing of the goods that were on the trucks or the fuel that was in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at a document relating to these trucks. That's 65 ter 25825. You'll see that this is a letter from the Sanski Most SJB chief, Mirko Vrucinic, to the president of the municipality enclosing a report on the condition of the trucks seized from Agrokomerc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the first paragraph states that a total of 29 vehicles were seized as you've described. And it states that at the beginning of the war, these vehicles were used for the transport of Agrokomerc vehicles to Zenica, Zavidovici, and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now if we could move to page 3 of the English and the B/C/S. At the bottom of the page in the English, it states that: "When they were seized they were parked -- all vehicles were parked in the grounds of the Sip which was put in charge of guarding them following an order of the Crisis Staff. Vinko Nikolic, a staff member, was in charge of the vehicles on behalf of the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So I ask you again, you personally were responsible for the use and the distribution of these vehicles that were seized on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see page 4 in the English. It's the same page on the B/C/S. And this discusses the distribution of these vehicles. It states that it was established that during that time trailer trucks were given for use to the following entities and individuals. And it goes on to list the 6th Brigade, a number of trucks, including two of the refrigerated trailers and one with a tarpaulin, the corps command or corps police, again, a truck with a refrigerated trailer, and the SOS sabotage platoon, who was -- which was issued with a number of vehicles, including one freight vehicle, with a semi-automatic gun mounted on top.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So it's true, isn't it, that you distributed these vehicles to the 6th Brigade, to the military police, and to the SOS?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the order of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, the truck with the semi-automatic gun mounted on it, this was used by the SOS in mop-up operations in Sanski Most; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only in the Vrhpolje and Hrustovo operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And some of the trucks that you appropriated were also used to transport Muslims out of the municipality; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since there were no other vehicles, we took the vehicles that were more suitable to transport people to Manjaca than the old ones that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now moving to a different topic, Mr. Nikolic. After -- in your response to question 12, you state that all citizens of Sanski Most, regardless of their ethnicity, were allowed to remain in their jobs if they respected the constitution of the Republika Srpska. But it's true, isn't it, that even before the Serb take-over of the municipality non-Serbs were being removed from their jobs. And, in fact, on the 28th of February, the SOS, your group, together with the SDS president Vlado Vrkic, forcibly removed the Croatian director of the SDK, that's the public auditing service; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was not forcibly. That was pursuant to an agreement with that lady who was a director. She was getting on. She was married to a Serb. And together with the president of the party, two or three of us wanted to take the keys of the strongholds, and they were kept by the three people who worked in the SDK. We went to fetch those keys and to bring them to the SDK building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we see P3397 again. And I'm interested this time in page 4 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we look towards the second half of the last paragraph in the English, and again it's towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S also. It states in your document that you signed: "We must also mention how we resolved a previous problem of the SDK." And it continues: "Despite Alija's police, they weren't all Alijas but that's what we now call them, so you Serbs won't hold it against me. We, fellow Serbs, carried out a raid on the Sanski Most SDK, took away the keys from the stubborn Croatian woman-director who refused any form of co-operation or agreement, and continued according to plan." So it's not true, is it, as you've just told this Court that this was pursuant to the agreement of the Croatian director. According to your own document, Mr. Nikolic, there was no agreement but, rather, you took over the SDK by force?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. We are having problems with interpretation. The word that was used was "attack" where it should have been "a forcible entry," so I'm not sure about the -- the interpretation. Perhaps the word that should have been used is "raid" or something. [In English] Original, third line from the bottom of this paragraph, "upad."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the witness should have understood in B/C/S correctly and then there should be no problem. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. At that time, which was in the month of February, I believe, in Sanski Most we had a joint police and joint authorities. The commander of the police was a Muslim. We couldn't carry weapons without being noticed by police officers of other ethnic groups and we could not stage any raids without being reported. We couldn't do anything of that kind by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we go further, Ms. McKenna, if you could ask the witness what this document was about. This titled as -- entitled as report, but it sounds like a speech. Mr. Nikolic, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a report about the work of the SOS in the months of January and February, as far as I can understand. And this was drafted by the SOS commander, the late Dusan Savic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would like us to clarify as we'll be referring to this document quite a bit, if we can go to the first page, it's evident that it's a report on the activities of the SOS between the 1st of May and the 16th of September, 1992. And as the witness has previously confirmed, it was signed by Dusan Savic himself and Goran Cankovic, all three of whom were the members of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this report starts with this: "Fellow Serbs, patriots, gentlemen..." It looks like an address in a public gathering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a form of address. This is the usual form of address for this kind of document, and it refers to anybody who is going to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, line 17, I'm not sure whether Madam McKenna said that that pertained to May 1991. It's September 1992. Either she omitted to say so or the transcript did not reflect her words. This refers to a period starting with May 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. From -- between May 1991 and September 1992. I leave it there. Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's turn to discuss the dismissals which took place after the events of 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And could we please see P3400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I'm sorry. Take a look at the first paragraph here. I'm not sure if it's legible on your part. The first paragraph, following, "Fellow Serbs, patriots, gentlemen," the first paragraph says: "You have chosen a bad time to argue and separate - do not look for a culprit where there isn't one." Who was "you" there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I can't see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it there again. Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We'll come back to this document, Mr. Nikolic, but I'd like it look at another document, which is P3400. And this, as you'll see are -- these are conclusions from a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most held on the 24th of April, 1992. At the bottom of the page, at number 8, it states: "Mladen Lukic, Vinko, and Boro are tasked with preparing the appointment of the acting director of the health centre in Sanski Most." Now, this Vinko, this is a reference to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And this position had formerly been held by a Muslim; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you and your colleagues filled this position -- filled it with a Serb within a matter of days; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, let's look at another meeting, which is P3649. These are conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, the meeting held on the 29th of April, 1992. And the first conclusion is that: "Changes be made and all officials at the municipal court of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most be appointed as acting official (Vrkes, Vrucinic and Nikolic are in charge of this)." Again, this is a reference to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now there's evidence before the Trial Chamber that this resulted in the replacement of all non-Serbs in the court, including Judge Nedzad Muhic, Azra Ubegovic [phoen], and Adil Draganovic. That's true, isn't it, they were all replaced?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We just replaced the president of the court, Mr. Draganovic. And he, because he was a member of the SDA party, was a nationalist, according to the evidence we had; whereas, the other judges probably left after he was dismissed from the service, of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: One of these judges who you claim left of their own will, Mr. Nikolic, Judge Nedzad Muhic, he was one of the victims who suffocated to death en route to Manjaca camp, one of those people who you term suspects. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not call him a suspect. I said that only about the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in your statement, when you're discussing the group of people who suffocated to death en route to Manjaca camp, you said that they were all suspects. There's evidence before this Trial Chamber that one of these people was Judge Nedzad Muhic, one of the judges that you assisted in replacing with a Serb. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's true we replaced only the president of the court. And as far as Nedzad is concerned, it was probably the police, because the police starts investigations of people who had weapons. And they must have accused him of that act.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now these people who suffocated to death during their transport to Manjaca, you say they suffocated due to the great heat and the lack of oxygen. That lack of oxygen was because they were being crammed into trucks with no ventilation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The trucks and the security were probably not ready for a transport of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And these were the trucks that you had distributed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not only those trucks. There were both buses and trucks in the transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Trucks for which you were responsible as the member of the Crisis Staff responsible for vehicles; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the paragraph number of his statement wherein he stated about the suffocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It is paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I have an old version. Please go --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's paragraph 21 in the old version. There were a number of changes to the paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I'd like to turn our focus to the SOS operations. Now, in response to question 28, you state that the SOS were not armed until April 1992. If we could go back to P3397, which is your report on the SOS activities. And I'd like to see pages 2 of the English and the B/C/S of this report, please. And it's the last paragraph in the B/C/S, and the fourth paragraph down in the English. And you're discussing in this report how the SOS kept the peace from May 1991, and you continue: "These young men, I'm thinking of the seven lads who tirelessly brought weapons from various warehouses and points and armed the Serbian people, risking that the weapons fall into the hands of Ustashas and Green Berets ..." So, in fact, Mr. Nikolic, the truth is that the SOS helped arm the Serbian people in Sanski Most before the crisis -- before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you talk -- excuse me. You talk in your statement about the chaos in Sanski Most. But it's true, isn't it, that the SOS was heavily involved in creating that chaos?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, Mr. Nikolic, that the SOS blew up buildings owned by Muslims and Croats in order to intimidate the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's not true. That was done by people who had explosives. And the only people who could have done that were the fighting men from the 6th Sana Brigade who were coming there on leave. Members of the SOS were detained by the police several times, and it was never proven that they had done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next page in the B/C/S and it's on the same page in the English. And it's in the second last paragraph in the English. And in the middle of the second paragraph in the B/C/S, Mr. Nikolic, you state: "Blowing up buildings was not in anyone's interest but we could not crush the Ustasha and Green Berets any other way." So it's true, isn't it, that the SOS was involved in the blowing up of buildings?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's not right in that context. It's different. Because we were there to keep the peace to prevent chaos from breaking out. And some individuals, taking advantage, probably did things like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, there's evidence before this Trial Chamber of SOS bombings of Muslim and Croat-owned buildings in 1991 and early 1992, including law offices and cafe bars. So it's not true that the SOS was there to keep the peace. The SOS, the pre-war role of the SOS, was to create havoc, to raise tensions, and to intimidate the non-Serb population of Sanski Most. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that the SOS assisted the SJB in taking Muslims and Croats into custody?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was only in the time after the Serbian take-over in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's discuss that time. In your response to question 30, you discuss the attacks on Bosnian Muslim neighbourhoods and villages in the municipality, including, in Mahala Hrustovo and Vrhpolje in which the SOS participated. And I'd like to direct your attention to page 5 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S of this document, please. It's very at the bottom of this page in the B/C/S and continues on to the next page, is a discussion of these operations that you mention in paragraph -- or at -- you deal with in response to question 30. And the document states: "After that, one combat action followed another, mopping up in Trnova, Mahala, Hrustovo, Vrhpolje (twice) and Marini. We caught seven extremist Ustashas, the corridor, 20 days, constant patrols around town." And you continue with a list of mopping up and clearing of the terrain of the last Ustasha and Green Berets? Now in response to question 28 you state that all -- from mid-May, all of the members of the SOS were placed under the command of the VRS. It's correct, is it, that during these mopping-up operations which we've just mentioned, the SOS was subordinated to the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you state that the operations were not planned in advance, and that during the attack on Mahala residents were evacuated to the sports hall in order to avoid civilian casualties. And that's in response to question 30 and question 31. In fact, Mr. Nikolic, there's evidence before the Trial Chamber that these operations were part of a planned, co-ordinated effort to attack those villages and neighbourhoods. And in this regard, I'd like to look at P3313. And this, you'll see, is the order from TO commander Nedeljko Anicic, and if you focus on number 4 which is -- item number 4 which is on page 2 of the B/C/S and at the bottom, and page 2 of the English as well. Anicic says: "I have decided ..." "After artillery preparations, disarm the settlements of Mahala, Otoka, Muhici, Marija Bursac, the Omladinsko neighbourhood, Aladzica [phoen] neighbourhood, in co-ordination with the 6th Brigade units in order to cause the enemy great human materiel and technical losses." And two paragraphs down it says: "Stand by for attack at 0500 on 26 May." And if we could just skip to page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. At the top of the page in B/C/S and under heading 15 in the English at the bottom, it states: "Upon completion of the task, take the prisoners to the sports hall of the secondary school centre, and hand over the war booty to the Sanski Most Serbian TO staff." So, in fact, this operation was a planned, co-ordinated TO and 6th Brigade attack, the aim of which was to cause great human, materiel, and technical losses. And the plan was not to evacuate civilians to the sports hall for their own safety, but rather to take the prisoners to the sports hall. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. Since the Muslim part of Sanski Most was armed and since the Green Berets had been observed in that part of Sanski Most, most probably the decision was taken to address to them an ultimatum and appeal to them to surrender their weapons. I believe that within 24 hours an appeal was made to surrender weapons and for these people who had been training those units to surrender themselves. However, when weapons were being turned over, most of the civilians of their own will left that area and we put them up at the gym, and some crossed the river Sana and found shelter with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at another document relating to this operation. That's P3928. I'd like you to look at the third paragraph down, and it states: "On 25th May, 1992, this 'disarming' was followed by a military action (attack) against the downtown neighbourhood of Mahala, which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians, but no significant amount of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier." So in the attack on Mahala, contrary to what you've just stated, no significant amount of weapons were found, and yet, despite this fact, 2.000 civilians were taken into custody. So, again, contrary to your contention, these citizens or civilians were not evacuated in order to avoid casualty. They were, according to this document, captured.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that all the civilians came out in time to the gym and the right bank of the river. It's a settlement with a population of several thousands. As for the weapons, the extreme men escaped to Vrhpolje village, taking their weapons with them. But we found out about that later, when the operation Vrhpolje and Hrustovo began.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's be clear about what happened in the operation at Mahala, Mr. Nikolic. There's evidence before this Trial Chamber that there was no organised resistance in Mahala, that Serb soldiers forced Mahala residents to gather in a field, Mahala was then shelled, and civilians, including those who were too weak or infirm to move, were wounded and were killed, and then following that shelling, houses were looted and burnt down. That's the truth of what happened in Mahala, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, there couldn't have been any use of large calibres because this was the centre of the town. Hand-held launchers and other infantry weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In your statement, you contend that there was no killing of civilians in the villages. That's in response to question 32. I'd like to look at P3635 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move away from this document, does this document itself refers to 2.000 civilians captured?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh yes, yes, yes. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this is a diary of another fellow Crisis Staff member, Nenad Davidovic. I'd like to look at page 29 of the English and the B/C/S, which is, as you will see in a moment, a record of the Crisis Staff meeting of the 30th of May. Now, on the 30th of May, you were still -- that was the day you were formally appointed to the Crisis Staff, so you would have attended this Crisis Staff meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And let's see what Mr. Davidovic noted. He -- under 2, it states: "Speeding up restoration in that Mahala, Otoka, and Muhici." A few bullet points down it states: "Collect all bodies in a single place. Exclude those who talk too much?" I'd like to turn to the next page, which is continued notes of this meeting. It states: "They will come for the bodies at 0900. "The Betonirka for identification. "Discusses measures of pest control. "Nylon cover on the ground." And then it states: "There is a possibility of dressing them in our uniforms." Now, this, Mr. Nikolic, was the Crisis Staff's attempt to cover up the killing of unarmed civilians by making them look like military personnel; that's correct, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, staying with the topic of killing of unarmed civilians, you've discussed how the SOS was involved in mopping-up operations in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje while it was subordinated to the 6th Brigade. There is evidence before the Trial Chamber that in Hrustovo, on the 31st of May -- 1st of May, in a co-ordinated attack by the 6th Brigade and local paramilitary formations, multiple civilians were killed, including unarmed women and children who were taking shelter in a garage. And in Vrhpolje, around that same time in another 6th Brigade attack, soldiers were rounded up -- excuse me, soldiers rounded up the inhabitants of Begici village, took them in to Vrhpolje bridge, forced them to jump off and opened fire on them, again killing multiple unarmed individuals in this operation. These were the kind of mopping-up operations that you and your unit and the 6th Brigade were involved in, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that description. The operation at Hrustovo also began with the surrendering of weapons by Muslim extremists. However, the first day, three soldiers from the 6th Sana Brigade were killed and then orders came from the brigade commander to begin with artillery attack at Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, which are two villages outside of Sanski Most. And it's probably during this artillery action that some civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at the operations specifically of the SDS -- or, excuse me, the SOS during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So could we please see D1681.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I have a remark to make. Could the Prosecutor tell us who created the first page of this diary and described Mr. Davidovic as a member of the Crisis Staff of the SDS? There is no such qualification in the manuscript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would refer Mr. Karadzic to P2614, which is the conclusions in which the Crisis Staff members were appointed. Mr. Davidovic is named as number 9 in that document, as the member in charge of municipal medical services. I'll continue. Could we please see D1681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This was -- just a second. This was admitted earlier on. But in that -- what's the answer to the first part of the question? Who -- as, i.e., who produced the first page of this typewritten page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll have to check that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And perhaps -- I note the time. Perhaps it's better if -- before I move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Should we take a break? Before that, yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It remains unclear. Was it the Crisis Staff the SDS or the municipal Crisis Staff? Where does the SDS come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see as -- first see who created this first page. Shall we take a break for half an hour and resume at three minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just with regard to the diary that we were discussing prior to the break, it was seized by the OTP in December 1996 in that format from the AID, Sanski Most, and it was confirmed by the -- the excerpts were confirmed by the witness, through him - it was tendered in this case - a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But no information as to who wrote the first page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No specific information as to who wrote the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before we come to the activities of the SOS, your own group, you make various assertions regarding the investigation centres and their professionalism of the officials who were taking statements of those centres. Now, there's -- and you state that no one was allowed to mistreat or beat the people from whom statements were taken. That's at -- in your response to question 22. There is a wealth of evidence before this Trial Chamber of such mistreatment and beatings. That includes Witness Mirsad Karabeg, who described being beaten at the SJB by prison guards on his head, his shoulders, back, the soles of his feet and his legs, and using their fists, feet, electric cable, wooden poles, and being given to civilians in order for the civilians to beat him as well. We also have evidence of witnesses who were subjected to the same kind of beatings at the Betonirka facility, including beatings with police batons, wooden chairs, and with sticks. So this is the reality of what was going on in Sanski Most, wasn't it? There were systematic beatings taking place at the detention centres and no one was being punished or prosecuted for them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Crisis Staff order the police not to resort to coercive measures. Now I know, I believe that there were certain situations, and I remember that a policeman was dismissed because he beat a detained person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's turn to the activities of your own group, the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see D1681.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, as you'll see, Mr. Nikolic, is a 5th of August, 1992 report from the SJB Sanski Most to the SJB Banja Luka. We're going to look at the first three paragraphs in some detail. The first paragraph states that: "In the last two months in Sanski Most municipality, there has been a great deal of activity by certain paramilitary groups that have broken free from the command of the army and conduct their own private operations that can be seen in the planting of explosives, the torching of houses, killings, lootings, and other types of crime against the Muslim and Croatian population, all aimed at acquiring material profit and putting pressure on them to move out." It continues: "In the last two months, 45 explosions have been set off at Muslim houses and business premises, two mosques have been destroyed, five buildings have been torched and four killings have been carried out." And the next paragraph states: "It is mostly small groups involved, primarily soldiers, and they operate outside the knowledge of their commands. To date, we have registered four such groups, among which there is the so-called SOS group, a former paramilitary group with a strength of around 30 men, which was formally placed under the command of the local military unit as a sabotage platoon but it is not under full control." Now, this is the group that you were a leading member of, a group known to be committing systematic crimes against non-Serbs, including the destruction of buildings, plunder, and killings in order to pressurise them to leave the municipality. This is your group, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can I just say this: This document is from the month of August. Our group, SOS, at the beginning of the month of June, went to the corridor, went into combat, so we were not in Sanski Most for a month. So some groups that introduced themselves as SOS at that time and did these things in town are people I don't know. We were far away from Sanski Most. We could not have done this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, your own document that you signed talks about the destruction of buildings in order to crush the Ustasha and the Green Beret. This contemporaneous document discusses the activities that your group was involved in while it was working under the subordination of the 6th Brigade. The reality is that while you talk about the fact that individuals who committed crimes being taken off the streets, no members of the SOS were prosecuted for these crimes that they were committing against non-Serbs. That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am telling you that we were far away at the front line. And this report speaks about the months of August and June and July that year, probably. We were not in town then at all. As SOS, we formally ceased to exist when we went to the corridor, and we were soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what the Major Brajic, the 6th Brigade Chief of Staff said at that time, and that's, again, in your document. That's P3397. And could we please see page 5 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. This is the passage after you've described the operations in which you were involved, the various mopping-up operations. And it states: "After we had completed the operation, we were called by Major Brajic who thanked us for our co-operation as though we were mercenaries or at worst a paramilitary formation." So this is the truth, isn't it, Mr. Nikolic, that your SOS group, which was known to be committing systematic and persecutory crimes against the non-Serb population of Sanski Most worked hand in hand with the Crisis Staff and was valued by the military authorities? That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember when this happened, after which operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you say that in response to question 12 you say that more than 8.000 Muslims continued to live in the Sanski Most municipality. Now, according to the 1991 census in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are over 28.000 Muslims in Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And for the parties' reference that's P6548, English page 6, and B/C/S page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: By February 1995, the Banja Luka State Security Department reported that 3.350 Muslims remained. And that's P5449. So it's not true, is it, that more than 8.000 Muslims remained? In fact, of a population of over 28.000, only 3.350 were left in 1995. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I was speaking about -- towards the end of the war, that maybe 8.000 inhabitants of Muslim ethnicity could still be living in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, repeatedly in your statement you talk about the voluntary nature of the departure of Sanski Most's non-Serbs. You say that the Muslim chose to leave, that -- in response to question 14, you say that people decided to voluntarily leave and the authorities had an obligation to help them. And in answer to question 24, you say that the civilian authorities, police and army, did not plan, instigate, or order the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly go back to the diary of Mr. Davidovic. That's P3635. And I'm interested in pages 42 of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And these are Mr. Davidovic's notes of a Crisis Staff meeting of the 8th of June, 1992, and if you could focus on conclusion number 4, it states: "Move the Muslims and Croats to the extent which would provide for a steady control of power." So this plan that was set out in early June, it clearly doesn't relate to a voluntary transfer, does it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. Most Muslims came to ask for transportation and for an escort in order to be able to get to Bihac or Jajce or across the Croatian border. That's why the Crisis Staff made such a decision, that the Muslims should move out but escorted by our army and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at meeting notes from two days later. And that's at English page 49 and B/C/S page 48. And these are the meeting notes of -- or notes of a meeting of 10th of June, and they state: "The job of deportation of a part of the Muslim population failed. Lot of mistakes. "Proposal: ... appoint a person for the deportation of part of the population ..." So, again, I put it to you that this deportation was clearly not voluntary. Whether or not the Muslims agree with it, Sanski Most Crisis Staff was requiring that these Muslims leave.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You continue to assert, Mr. Nikolic, that the voluntary -- that the departure of non-Serbs from Sanski Most was entirely voluntary. Today, we've discussed the destruction of Muslim villages in Sanski Most municipality by Serb forces, including the VRS, the TO, and your own group, the SOS, from late May. We've discussed how these villages were attacked, buildings were destroyed, and civilians were killed. We've seen evidence of the mass detention of civilians, we've talked about people being crammed into trucks and suffocating to death en route to their detention in Manjaca camp, and we have seen evidence of the systematic crimes that your own group, the SOS, committed against non-Serbs in order to pressurise them to leave the municipality, both before and during the war. So in the face of this evidence of persecuting and systematic abuse that non-Serbs living in these circumstances were subjected, there is no way in which their departure could be considered voluntary, is there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, probably under these circumstances and in fear for their lives, most of them decided to ask us to secure their journey so that they could go to their own territory, Muslim-held territory, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McKenna. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, let us start with the latest. In line 3, it was stated that Muslim villages in Sanski Most were destroyed. Can you tell us roughly how many Muslim villages there are in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I think about 15 or so. Over 15. I don't know the exact number. But there are quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'll try to put the question this way: Brdari, is that a predominantly Muslim village, or perhaps the number is equal, Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the number is equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Brdari destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Caplje, is that a predominantly Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Caplje destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Demisevci, is that an almost purely Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is the purest of them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Dzevar, is that a predominantly Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Muslims and Serbs and Croats live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Dzevar destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Fajtovci, is that a predominantly Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Gorice, is that a predominantly Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, there is Gornji Kamengrad and Donji Kamengrad. Are most -- are both of them predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting in either one of the Kamengrads?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was any one of them destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Hrustinovci? That is -- Hrustinovci is mixed, and Hrustovo is Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Hrustovo is Muslim, predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Krkojevci, is that predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All three ethnicities, all three religions are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Modra predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Okrec?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is predominantly Muslim, a predominantly Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Podbrijezje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's a neighbourhood, a suburb of Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Similar to Mahala?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A bit further away from the centre, but it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have to pause. Please do pause. So you say it's similar to Mahala but a bit further away. Was Podbrijezje destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, Podvidaca. What's that like?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Part of it is Serb. And just before you enter Podvidaca, there's a Muslim hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Skucani Vakuf, what about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Stari Majdan?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslim, but there were Serbs and Croats there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The ones that I mentioned, Skucani Vakuf, Stari Majdan, were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sehovci?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sehovci, well, a few houses were torched, as far as I heard, but it wasn't that there was any combat there or destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber now what the difference is between these that were not destroyed and where there was no fighting and Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, Trnova, and these other ones, and Mahala?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, to the best of our knowledge, Mahala, Vrhpolje, and Hrustovo had about 900 persons of Muslim ethnicity who were armed. And the Green Berets came for training there. They came from Bihac and Sarajevo. And that is probably why there was fighting there. And that's why these Muslim forces there were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From when did these armed formations exist? When did you find out about that? And when did you find out that they were armed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Already at the end of 1991, around September 1991, the army, the then-army of the SFRY and the 6th Sana Brigade, went into combat in Croatia. Since there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs there at the time, the next day, all the Muslims and Croats left the brigade and returned to Sanski Most with their weapons. And probably, from that time onwards, they started arming themselves intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D5 which is a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why were the Serbian Defence Forces set up?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The entire 6th Sana Brigade was on the front line and all the combatants were of Serb ethnicity. Several people of Serb ethnicity from Sanski Most went to the brigade and only old and infirm Serbs remained in town. That's why a decision was reached to set up the SOS to protect the remaining population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the document which was drafted in March 1992. On the 7th of March, 1992, was the MUP still united, and was the state security still one?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the text in the Serbian on the left-hand side to see what the state security learned. You don't have to read it aloud, but please look at the names. It says that they are very impertinent and aggressive. People who are mentioned are Arif and Izet Huranovic from Vrhpolje, about 500 armed civilians and about 3.000 Muslims who own long barrels. Could you please read the names of those who were involved in the activities as the main players?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The mainly responsible for the SDA were Ismet Sarcevic, a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. Putting the document in this way and asking him to read from it is clearly a leading way of conducting Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, I don't see the point. Just ... Could you not put your question first, Mr. Karadzic, without asking the witness to read out the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know the names of the prominent extremists in Sanski Most? You were already asked about that during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from the state security and the crime prevention police in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about their conduct? Was it very public and visible?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They requested money from other Muslims to buy weapons from their -- for their units. There were a lot of examples of Muslims who wanted our protection because they were threatened and they didn't want to give them money, and they didn't want to participate in those organised activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there prominent Muslims who were different and who are not on this list?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the names of those who were recognised in March as the key players in the exercise to arm the 3.000 Muslim citizens?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Ismet Sarcevic, a lawyer; Suad Sabic, a lawyer; Adil Draganovic, president of the court; Revzid Kurbegovic, president of the SDA board; Mirzet Karabeg, chairman of the Sanski Most Executive Committee; and Enver Burnic, commander of the Sanski Most police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when it comes to his Excellency's question about the purpose, I would like to remind you that some of the people on this list came to testify against me as OTP witnesses. They testified as if they were neutral witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a useless comment. In asking -- he just read out this document. So how does it help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- my question is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fact that the state security which was still a joint institution, how did it tally with your experiences on the eve of the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We knew all that because the state security monitored the situation closely and they knew who it was that armed the Muslims, who organised the purchase of the weapons, and obviously since I knew a lot of people and I was friends with many of them, they told me about that, and that's how we learned that they were preparing themselves for a showdown with the Serbs, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a while ago, you accepted the possibility that there were individual cases of ill-treatment, although Madam McKenna suggested that that ill-treatment was systematic. According to what you know, what was the attitude of the authorities towards the abuse of power during interrogation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at all the meetings, it was demanded from the police to comply with the law when interrogating Muslim extremists. As far as I know, that's how they, indeed, behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the attitude of the authorities towards the perpetrators of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I remember a situation when a policeman was removed from his job and transferred to another job once it was learned that he had ill treated a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the position or attitude towards expulsion and intimidation. A little while ago, we saw in the diary that the deportation failed. What was the position of the authorities towards the intimidation and expulsion of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the meetings that I attended at the Crisis Staff, the emphasis was always placed on protecting all the civilians, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. It was also emphasised that houses should not be burned or destroyed and that Muslims should not be killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown D1680.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that these are minutes? Please look at the document. We now have the translation as well. So this is the Executive Committee, which means that the Crisis Staff no longer existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 3 in Serbian or, rather, page 4 in Serbian and page 3 in English. Please pay attention to the second paragraph in the Serbian. Kalacun says: "I would like to ask the chairman of the Executive Committee to inform us of the general position of the AR Krajina government on the exodus from the Serbian state." Kalacun -- can we see it in English as well? Yes, we can. It is the fourth paragraph from the top of the page. And now can you see Rasula's response?
