First of all, is it the position of the government at Pale that is requested or the position of the government of the autonomous region? What is Kalacun requesting here? Please look at the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. Once again, Mr. Karadzic is just getting the witness to read from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, yes. Do you follow the point raised by Ms. McKenna, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to read - you don't have to do it aloud - what Mr. Rasula said in respond both, Rasula and Lukic, as a matter of fact. And could you please tell us how this tally with your experience and what you knew about the position of the government.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what we in the Crisis Staff wanted to protect the Muslim civilians and to prevent further exodus. We wanted the Muslims to remain living in the Serbian state, and I believe that the same thing is said here in this document. The position of the Crisis Staff was always that as few Muslims should move out and for a majority of them to remain living in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how does this tally what you know? It says here that the authorities don't have the money for the fuel.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it's only normal. There was no fuel. There was a war going on. There was no forceable removal of the population. If somebody wanted to forcibly remove them, conditions would have been put in place for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that the phone lines were down, that the roads were blocked, and so on and so forth. When it comes to those meetings, either of the Crisis Staff or the SOS, did you receive an instruction from either Pale or the government or the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. On the day or during the night when the municipality was liberated, all the communications were down. The commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic, arrived with his subordinates into town, and that's the only thing that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up page 5 in English and page 7 in Serbian, in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top, it says that you and the public security station are tasked with something. What is it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was a member of the 6th Sana Brigade. Mladen Lukic was the president of the executive board at the time, and he tasked us with establishing the number of Agrokomerc trucks that had been on loan and participated in the activities to transport goods. He wanted us to take stock of all the trucks that were missing and their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what Agrokomerc is, where it was based, and whether we were at war with the entity at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Agrokomerc was based in Velika Kladusa, in the Cazin region, with a majority Muslim population, Bihac was its centre, and all the arming and all the Green Berets started from there in the direction of Sanski Most and other Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak up. Could you please speak more slowly. And I would like to remind both myself and you that we should pause between my questions and your answers. Thank you. So how were the movable assets belonging to Agrokomerc treated? Were they treated as private, as war booty, or what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was considered war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to war booty, was it regulated by the law?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now could you please look at the second paragraph -- or, rather, the second half of paragraph 3. The resettlement for any persons who express wish and have the necessary documents or telex message in which they are guaranteed accommodation should be made possible. Could you please tell us -- or interpret this paragraph for us, rather.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can give you my opinion. At that time, I was deployed on the front line. I suppose the idea was to know where those Muslims are headed and what their destination was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the month of August. I believe that you already returned by then.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was probably on furlough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we bring up 65 ter 1569 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we move on, could you expand on -- on your understanding of this paragraph, which says: "For any person who expresses the wish and has the necessary documents ... voluntary resettlement will be made possible."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please ask the witness to read the document? Because the interpretation is, again, not good -- or, rather, the translation is not good, because the English translation is, again, not good, and I would like the interpreters not to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But could we go back to page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, I believe it's 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Do you see the words of Mr. Stojinovic after Lukic's intervention? Could you read out aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To enable the people who wish to leave our republic, and the competent authority should continue working on the issuance of loyalty."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to the last page. Yes. If you could read aloud the paragraph we discussed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Enabling voluntary moving out for all persons who expressed their desire to do so and are in possession of the necessary documentation, i.e., have a telex guaranteeing their accommodation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And now you could tell us how you understood this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a reference to voluntary moving out, not forced evacuation. It says: "Those who expressed the desire to leave town."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, one of the requirements is for people to show that they have some accommodation guaranteed for them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were supposed to show that somebody in the Muslim-held area will provide them with accommodation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? Oh, it has been admitted. So I asked for 55 -- 65 ter 5169. 5169 is the one I wanted. I don't think this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 1D number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now we have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to wait for the Serbian version, but I'll read to you ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Registry is obviously facing constraints of the same kind that I do all the time. Now we have the Serbian version without the English. Okay. They're both here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this document? What is it about and what's the date? Let me help you. At the top we read: The Co-ordinating Committee of the Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Municipal Assembly, 4 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karadzic begins to potentially lead the witness with this document, it would be good if he could lay a foundation for the use of the document. I don't believe he has done so yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I did when I asked the witness what the attitude was towards intimidation, persecution of non-Serbs. That was the basis for my questions on several documents on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at item 2: "Report on the measures taken in the course of the investigation linked with a murder of Croatian civilians in Kruhari and Skrljevita." Are these Croatian villages, Kruhari?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kruhari was mixed Serb/Croat. And Skrljevita is a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 5 related to what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you should ask the witness whether he himself attended this meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the passage after point 5, the participants. Do you know them? I don't see your names here.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board had been already established by that time, and these people were capable of dealing with things under those circumstances: Nedeljko Rasula, as president of the municipality; Vlado Vrkes was president of the party; Mirko Vrucinic was chief of the police station; Boro Tadic was in the Territorial Defence, I believe; Milenko Delic was the public prosecutor; Rajko Stanic was president of the court. These are the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in item 2, do you see towards the bottom, they discuss the events in Skrljevita and Kruhari.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just what -- could you not put your question first to the witness about this murder of Kruhari and Skrljevita before showing the document to the witness. That was your point, Ms. McKenna, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour. The witness wasn't confirmed that he was at this meeting, and so showing him document is simply leading him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really disagree. The witness has already testified about efforts made by the authorities to prosecute and arrest people for murders of non-Serbs so he said that that was their policy. Now Dr. Karadzic is entitled to show him documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He could have asked about the murders of these individuals, in particular, whether the witness knew or not. And then depending upon the answers, he made proceed to put this document to the witness instead of just feeding him with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But even if the witness didn't know anything about those particular murders, he is entitled to put a document to the witness and ask him whether this -- how this tallies with his belief of the attitude towards to authorities whether he was present at the meeting or not. I agree that those things are relevant to the weight, but the way he is going about doing it, there's nothing leading about it, just to simply show a document to a witness and ask him to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the way Mr. Karadzic put his question was a bit different from the way you suggested so far. Please continue, bearing in mind what we just discussed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know the participants of this meeting whose names you read out a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was their attitude as representatives of the authorities towards crimes and intimidation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They worked for reducing the incidents of intimidation and murders in Sanski Most. I know that because I knew personally the president of the court and the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about that killing of civilians in Kruhari, Skrljevita?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it so happens that I was on sick-leave that month because I had been wounded, and I heard about some killing involving several victims in these villages which were several kilometres away from the town. The police searched and I think they found the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the names of those who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew this man Kajtez is his last name. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we finish with this, you were asked on page 24 -- no, 25, or something like that, about how the police treated a certain group that held themselves out to be the SOS. Did the SOS expel anyone for a certain type of conduct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were members of the SOS and others who didn't want to go to war and did everything to avoid it. And the brigade command, of course, expelled such people, took their weapons away, and they remained in Sanski Most. And such groups called themselves SOS because that made it easier for them to do certain things around town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show page 3 in both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at items 11 and 12, and tell us if you know anything about this. How does this fit in with your knowledge and your experience concerning the way the authorities treated such things?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Some people were using Muslim cafes and businesses that had been abandoned, and that caused a lot of problems among citizens and the army and incidents of shooting, so the municipality authorities decided to deal with it in this way, by prohibiting the leasing of such businesses to minimise the incidents of such situations in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the next page be shown in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 6. What is paragraph 6 about? And is it consistent with your knowledge about the way the authorities treated such incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: One second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna. Let's collapse the document for the moment. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Once again, in asking the witness to read the paragraph and then comment on it, Mr. Karadzic is leading the witness. He is feeding the answers to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, are we not on the same topic still? It's continued? I think it's okay. Shall we continue? Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, look at paragraph 6, the first part, and tell me is it consistent with what you know and what was the attitude of the authorities towards incidents of looting, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I said already talking about the session of the Crisis Staff there were constant efforts to protect Muslim property from arson and from looting. And you see in this paragraph that this work continued, when the municipal authorities had been established and started to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last document on this topic, the treatment of non-Serbs, 65 ter 5180. The last document on this subject. So this is dated 9 December 1992. Look at paragraph 2 of item 2, where it is noted that in the territory of our municipality, problems are starting to be dealt with and the rule of law has been established. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All that the Executive Board did in October and November was towards imposing the rule of law and avoiding nationalist excess on both sides, and these people whom I know to be honest, these members of the Executive Board, have probably contributed to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does it tally with your experience that these families who wished to leave may do so and the return of those who wished to return is also allowed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The decision was clear, that they may return on the condition that they observe the laws of our republic. Those who wished to return, may return, and their property would be protected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph -- or, rather, item 4 to broadcast this decision at Radio Sanski Most. Look at items (a) and (b); to protect non-Serb settlements, and the public security station is made responsible to develop a protection plan to organise village guards and patrols. Mr. Mile Dobrijevic testified here that every Muslim village, each one of these, was assigned a policeman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is the point of referring to the other witness's evidence here at this moment? Reading out this sentence and referring to other witness's evidence, where are you heading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to see whether the witness knew about that and whether that is in line with this document, whether this was well known as a stand, and whether it was implemented. I thought that perhaps it wasn't phrased properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is your knowledge about the protection of villages, Muslim and Croat villages, in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I said, I was in Sanski Most at the time, and I knew about a great many things, and I knew that the police did everything to protect villages that had a predominantly Croat or Muslim population. They organised patrols, they brought them things that they were lacking for personnel hygiene and flour, and they protected them, and the municipality said that they should be assisted in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page of this document. If you could read out -- read aloud the first sentence in paragraph 1, item number 1. It ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can barely see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can -- can you read now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "It is allowed for the population to move out in an organised way from the areas of Trnovo, since they do not have conditions for continuing to live in this settlement, as well as families of extremists in this war. Other citizens who wish to leave the municipality may" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's sufficient. It says that there are no conditions for further life in that settlement, i.e., Trnovo. So one can say they are forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Trnovo is a smallish local commune that was poor even before the war, and probably -- I mean, people did not have the bare necessities, and they asked to move out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the authorities make life poor in Trnovo or did they make it more difficult in any way?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the village was a poor one before the war, and the authorities helped as much as they could during those months of war operations, and probably these inhabitants did not have enough or they were afraid of something; so, quite simply, they had to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested on page 24 of today's transcript that the SOS participated in explosions and that explosions happened at facilities owned by the non-Serb population. What is your knowledge? Where did explosions take place? When did they start?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were explosions in Serb, Muslim, and Croat properties. I think that this started in October and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D3906. Could that please be shown to the witness in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this. This is the 6th of December, 1991. The public security station. 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Request to publish a statement on explosions in the Sanski Most municipality." Can you tell us about this? For instance, the first one. On the 3rd of November, 1991, a rifle grenade from some distance on the Laro catering establishment owned by Nenad Majkic. What is his ethnic background, Majkic's?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next one is owned by Marko Beljic. What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's not Bejlic, it's Reljic. And this is also a Serb who had a restaurant, an exclusive restaurant at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 15 should not be Q, it should be A. What about the next one, Kaurinovic, Marko?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kaurinovic, he's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for Veljic, it didn't say Nenad Majkic, Serb. Now, Reljic? Reljic.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Reljic, Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from -- chronologically, we first have a Serb then another Serb and then a Croat?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, could you not put your question first instead of showing the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I think that I've already put my question. When did this start and whose shops exploded and now see a document, an authentic document that first it was the Christians, the shops owned by Christians, two Serbs and a Croat. You can see that chronologically. So obviously the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you asked ahead of this document to the witness was about the participation of SOS in explosions and explosions that happened at facilities owned by non-Serb population. So you could have asked the witness whether he knew any incident which happened in the facilities owned by Serbs, et cetera. You're just feeding the witness with this document, which is very leading and of low probative value, if at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, I am leading this. I'm saying in whose shops. And the witness said those owned by Serbs, Croats and Muslims. And now I'm trying to see whether the police said that the SOS were the perpetrators. But I cannot deal with that until we've had a look at all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or, actually, I will ask you. Did the police accuse the SOS for these explosions?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, they were interviewed, but there was no proof --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please repeat your answer but loudly and slowly.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The police brought in for questioning two of three of us from the SOS and told us that there had been explosions. However, we did not take part in that. They had no proof against us, and we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any of the perpetrators identified?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I heard, a few were arrested because a bomb or grenade was thrown in front of the shops, and these were drunken soldiers, former soldiers who came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the subject I'd like to ask you about a document which was shown to you. It is P3397. Was the value of the SOS being challenged? Were there any arguments provided? Or, rather, were there any arguments in the sense of quarrels about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be called up for the witness, P3397.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I think the witness can answer the question without reference to document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't follow the question itself. Could you put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any challenges concerning the value of the SOS? Did anyone bring it into question before it became the intervention platoon, or after that? Did that kind of thing happen? Were you in a position to defend the reputation of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. The authorities did not challenge us in any way because what we did was aimed at protecting the population. I already said that the 6th Sana Brigade was at the front line. They weren't in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 4 now, please. I'm actually trying to follow up what His Excellency Judge Kwon said. So please take a look at this page, the bottom of the page, where it says, "Dear brothers, do not allow," et cetera, et cetera, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's the same objection. If Mr. Karadzic is seeking to elicit evidence from the witness, he should elicit it rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He -- Mr. Karadzic says he was going to deal with the point I raised. Let us see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Dear brothers," that's what it says here. If you cannot see it, I'm going to read it out for you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You cannot really see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up here it says: I underline this once again, this is a confidential report and please bear that in mind. "Dear brothers, this is the beginning of the war and the bullet is still the judge, so do not permit" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Brothers." Yeah, at the beginning of -- fifth, sixth line in the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S? All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Low.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "So do not permit active-duty officers to go around the streets, and I don't know what state, offering war to whom? A Serb. It's unheard of." Now can you tell us what this is? What this is a reference to, that some officers are offering something that is improper?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There was some active-duty officers who offered weapons, even sold weapons. They did a lot of things that are improper for a Serb officer. And we wrote that in that context. Whoever uses such situations for their own material benefit will not be welcome there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about dismissals from work. Was it possible for Muslims and Croats to work in the Serb municipality of Sanski Most -- or, rather, did they have to transfer to the Muslim municipality and why were some of them dismissed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the dismissals took place because people found out that Muslim extremists took part in arming and the reselling of weapons and that's probably why they were dismissed, and they were brought in for questioning to the public security station. Also, quite a few professors, teachers, judges then -- in a state organisations. Of course, Muslims just stayed on and worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that policemen could stay on at the station. What about those who did not stay on? Did they have an alternative? Was the Muslim municipality supposed to have the same organs like the Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were negotiations, and an offer was made to the Muslim SDA to create a Muslim municipality in the offices of Sipad, Sanski Most, on the left bank of the Sana river. However, they did not agree to that. Afterwards, they took their weapons from the public security station and they went to the municipality building of Sanski Most. They barricaded themselves there, and they stayed on there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In April, on the 22nd of April, 1992, were you a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D16789. Actually D. D, it's D. D176 -- no. 1D1679. It's D. [In English] D1678. Sorry, sorry, 9. 1679.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, do take a look at this. Paragraph 7. Do you remember this? Were you at this meeting on the 22nd of April? And what is your position? What did know about this position vis-a-vis the Muslims and Croats and their rights?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was present at that meeting. And Boro and Vlado - Vlado Vrkes as president of the party; and Boro Savanovic, I think that was his last name, he was on the executive board - they were in charge of talks with the Muslim delegation. And they offered them all the rights that they were supposed to have at the workplace and in town in the municipality and the police. However, they did not agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the outcome of those talks? Who were the Muslims that they could talk to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Obviously they could talk to these, but there was another wing that did not want to take part in those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Obviously they could not talk to these, but there was moderate group. [Interpretation] You said "moderate," did you not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could the witness please be shown P3306.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please speak up and speak slowly. So P3306. Do you remember whether you attended this meeting of the Crisis Staff on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the first paragraph where it says that the talks were interrupted with extremists and that talks will continue with honest Muslims. How does this tally with what you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The witness has just said he didn't attend the meeting. So now Mr. Karadzic is just telling him what happened at the meeting and leading him in his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm asking the witness whether he knew anything about that. He did not have to attend the meeting. What was the position of the authorities vis-a-vis. He just said a while ago that they couldn't talk to the extremists but that they could talk to those who were moderate. And he said that without being prompted by either my question or the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the end of the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the witness is -- that the transcript is clear as to what the witness said in relation to who he could talk to. It says -- the witness says: Obviously they could not talk to these, but there was a moderate group that did not want to take part in these talks. Perhaps the witness could clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problems lies in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear the accused's intervention while conferring with my colleagues. The Chamber saw no problem with the accused's way of proceeding, in this case. But I'm about to read what Mr. Karadzic said. Probably you could repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, on page 66, we had a problem with the transcript. And I understand and I see where Ms. McKenna is coming from. On line 4, it was misrecorded. The witness said that they could not talk to those people but there was a moderate wing, and that was not recorded. The moderate wing was not recorded and it was also not recorded that those people could not be talked to. That's why I wanted to correct the transcript at the time. And now I have just asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, do you confirm that this is correct? Who were the people who were ready to talk with the Serbs and who weren't?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I confirmed that the leadership of the SDA could not be talked to about peace but there was another group of people who were more moderate and it was possible to talk to them, but their decision would not have meant anything to the rest of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just to finish this paragraph off, what about the talks with the Catholic parish priest, the effendi, and the Serbian Orthodox priest?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those were the talks involving all the three religious groups in order to try and calm the situation down, to calm down the population in order to avoid murders, killings, and chaos in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The word "effendi" was not recorded, but you did say all the three religious groups?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, all the three religious groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now the last question with regard to something Ms. McKenna asked you about: Mahala. Could you please tell us what was the position of the authorities, the police, and the armed forces vis-a-vis the population, including the enemy, the wounded, and the prisoners of war? Were there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that -- before that, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- attempts to cover things up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your question with respect to this document, Exhibit P3306?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was and the witness answered. I just wanted to show whether the contents of the document confirm what the witness said, that the talks with the extremists were abandoned and that the authorities opted for talks with others, including religious leaders. And he answered to that effect even before I displayed the documents. I just wanted to corroborate his words with the document and the document has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document. And before that, a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were things covered up, the abuses of power covered up, or perhaps crimes or breaches of discipline that happened during the operations against Mahala?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. The police did as best as they could at the time. They wanted to protect the population and their property, their apartments and houses, in that part of the town. That's how it was. All the police could do was enter that part of the town and protect the facilities. The civilian population could only return a few days later because there were the corpses of dead animals that had been killed or died, so the sanitisation had to be taken first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened to those who were killed or wounded from the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know that few were killed and that they were buried according to their religious rites in attendance of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any of the incidents or crimes covered up?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown D1810.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report issued by the municipal civilian protection staff on the 1st of May about the field inspection in Mahala and it says here that those who were wounded were attended by medical personnel, that a male corpse was found and identified as Dr. Alagic and buried, under eight. How does that tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Everything was done to end the situation in the best possible way and to avoid any controversial situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one very brief point, to clarify an issue that you raised yourself in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Ms. McKenna:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it's on the issue of the documentation for departure, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see P3307.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in your re-examination, you stated that documentation was required in order to show that departing Muslims had somebody to stay with or somebody in the Muslim-held area that would provide them with accommodation and that was the documentation that was required. I'd just like to show you -- you see that this is a decision on the criteria for the possibility of departure from the municipality dated the 2nd of July, 1992. And the first paragraph it states that voluntary departure from Sanski Most municipality shall be allowed to families and persons who give a statement, that they are permanently leaving the municipality and that they are leaving their real property to Sanski Most municipality. And if you turn your attention to article 4, it states that: "The municipal Secretariat for People's Defence shall give such peoples -- persons, the necessary permit to leave Sanski Most municipality on the basis of a statement or contract, if there are no legal obstacles." So this is the documentation that was being discussed in that meeting of the Crisis Staff, wasn't it, the documentation that was given when people who were leaving their municipality signed over their properties to the Sanski Most Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. This is a document which was issued by the Crisis Staff, and it predates the other document by three or four months. And that document was issued by the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most, and we're talking about two completely different bodies here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to seek clarification. When it comes to handing over property in this way, was it actually ceding ownership of that property?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't you leave it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Nikolic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Since we're going to have a lunch break, we'll rise all together. We'll resume at 22 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you're going to answer my questions in Serbian, I would kindly ask you to make a pause after my question to give the interpreters enough time to interpret our words. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, please make a pause. You understand Serbian and you answer in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D09816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, as you can note from the transcript, which is in front of you, since you gave your answer while Mr. Karadzic's question was being translated, your answer was not noted. So please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I have given statement to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D09816.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement. I see it in both languages, in the Serbian language and also translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be reminded to pause after Mr. Karadzic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I signed only the Serbian version, not the English, but I presume since Serbian is my native language that is the one that has correct importance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still too fast, both of us, and I again remind you to pause after my question. Dr. Davinic, does this statement accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as were put to you when your statement was given, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to read in English a short summary of Dr. Prvoslav Davinic's statement. [In English] Dr. Prvoslav Davinic was a United Nations official responsible for disarmament and security issues from 1976 till 1999. During the period 1992 to 1995, Dr. Davinic headed the United Nations Centre for Disarmament. He later served as minister of Defence for Serbia and Montenegro during the years, 2004 and 2005. He is now retired. Mr. Davinic learned of the 28th of August, 1995, shelling of the Markale marketplace during a morning briefing at the United Nations headquarters in New York head by Under-Secretary General for Political Affairs, Marrack Goulding. From that briefing, a subsequent report and a conversation with an UN colleague, Dr. Davinic believed that for political reasons, the United Nations wanted to ensure that the investigation concluded that the attack came from the Serb side. Mr. Davinic first met President Karadzic in March 1993 and met him for a second time in the first half of 1996 in Pale. In that 1996 meeting, President Karadzic was adamant that the Serbs had not fired the shell which landed on the Markale marketplace on 28th of August, 1995, and said that General Mladic had assured him that the UN and the Serb side had not fired -- assured him and the UN that Serb side did not fire that shell. And that is a short matter. At that moment, I do not have additional questions for Dr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Davinic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you have noted, sir, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that my understanding from your statement is that over the last 20 years, you've only met Dr. Karadzic twice - right? - the first time for about half an hour, and the second time after he was actually indicted for the crimes that he is now in custody on; right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to meet him a few more times in the interim. But at that time he was a fugitive, and I did not publicise the -- the fact that I had an opportunity to meet him during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even though you didn't say it in your statement, you've actually met Dr. Karadzic far more than just two times, just the two times that you disclosed in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But it was not relevant to my testimony which I am about to give today. Therefore, I didn't think it was relevant and this was the reason why I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, since we have this new information, actually, I -- I'd like to give you an opportunity to tell us about these meetings with Dr. Karadzic at the time he was a fugitive. So tell us when your first meeting with Dr. Karadzic was after he was indicted?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: The first meeting was actually in June 1996 in Pale, and I think that I referred to this in my written statement, and I confirm it now to you, and I met him in his home. There was no particular problem in accessing him. It was at his invitation through a mutual friend who knew him, and that friend knew, of course, me, and Dr. Karadzic expressed an interest in meeting me because he wanted to follow up on our meeting which took place in -- in the UN at the time when he was attending a peace conference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: And I referred to this in my statement. He visited my office. We spent one hour discussing various issues of relevance to what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now this meeting in 1996 --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- took place at a period of time where you were actually still serving as head of DDA; correct?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but this meeting with Dr. Karadzic had nothing to it with my official function at that time. I was actually en route to Sarajevo for total different purpose and I passed through Pale, and it was then possible to see him in accordance with a prior arrangement through this friend of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was that mutual friend?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: It was Dr. Predrag Stevanovic, medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And when was the next time you met Dr. Karadzic while he was a fugitive from justice?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I think it was later that year, I believe, September or October of that year. I was, again, going to a meeting in -- in Sarajevo, and on the way to Sarajevo, I again made a stop-over and I saw him briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want me to repeat what I said, or you managed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. Let's continue. Thank you, Mr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at that time, you met him at his home?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what did you discuss during that second meeting with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: This was a relatively short meeting and we did not really discuss much at that time because I was in a hurry to reach my destination. He was already in the situation in which he was, and we simply greeted each other, I wished him well, and I went off to my final destination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was the next time? So that would be the third time you met with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: But that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've only met him, then --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Three times all together --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- while he was a fugitive from justice?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, once I met him in New York and twice as he was fugitive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And knowing that Dr. Karadzic was a fugitive from justice, knowing and keeping in mind that you were at that time a senior-level UN official, knowing that Dr. Karadzic's surrender to this Tribunal would have the potential for great economic and other effects in the region, you must have advocated to Dr. Karadzic that he surrender himself, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was quite misleading. Because at the time, 1996, there were not these economic benefits to the region that were being talked about. So there were elements to that question that were not really very correct. But since he has answered it, we can leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Karadzic's response?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: His response was that he was considering all options. I might add, ma'am, if you would allow me, Your Honour, that, at that time, the fact that he was fugitive was not widely known. To my mind, I -- if I recall correctly, he was indicted shortly before the Dayton peace process started, but this indictment was made public much later. I also would like to point out that although I met him in my private capacity, I informed high-level officials in the UN of this meeting with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where is your report on the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, it was oral report because it was private meeting and did not require usual procedure of writing down such kind of reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I might come back to that. But while we're on the subject of meetings with Dr. Karadzic, in terms of the two meetings that you described in your statement and even, in fact, the one you've just told us about, you really just -- your written evidence, the evidence you've just given, really just repeats what he told you at that time, nothing further; right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: In one part it does; in another part, it brings in slightly additional information. But -- but, say, new information or different from what Dr. Karadzic and I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You would know, I suppose, because of your very senior position at the UN that Ambassador Yasushi Akashi served as the SRSG for the UN mission in the former Yugoslavia in 1994 and 1995. You know that?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I should know because I replaced Mr. Akashi as the head of the Centre for Disarmament Affairs. And I was for many years his special assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. And, so, you would have been aware that as the SRSG, Ambassador Akashi was frequently engaged in discussions and meetings and negotiations with the leadership of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That was outside the purview of my responsibilities in the UN. I didn't really follow it closely. I follow it only to the extent I got information from media and it concerned my country, and that was of importance to me to know how the peace process was going on. But I was not following it directly or in discussions with Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know -- maybe I wasn't clear. But you would agree with me that his job was to sit and negotiate with the leaders of the warring factions; right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I presume that was his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you said you were his special assistant for many years?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But not at the time when he was in charge of civil mission, peace-keeping mission in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I suppose then, though, you don't know that when Ambassador Akashi came here to testify in this trial to give evidence for Dr. Karadzic he confirmed that his experience with Dr. Karadzic was that in negotiations Dr. Karadzic had a tendency to twist the truth rather nonchalantly?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that and I'm not interested in his description of Mr. Karadzic and his behaviour. I had my own impression which I tried to describe in this statement which you have not come to it yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm happy to come to it.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I hope you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to come to my March 1993 and your meeting with Dr. Karadzic. You mentioned that that was in the context of what was happening in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I just want to talk about the context for a minute, and I'd like to establish it by having a look at what the Security Council understood was happening at that time, in March 1993, all right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter number 01207.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And I would -- and I would like to see the reference about the quotation of Ambassador Akashi. I do not remember that he said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That can be found at Defence Exhibit 3489. That's in page 80 of the actual book itself. And we only tendered a number of pages but the whole book has been uploaded for some reason, so that's why I cite to page 80 of the actual book, but D349, and also transcript pages 37757 to 37759 that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But now to get to the matter at hand. Dr. Davinic, just at the bottom of this page that you see, there's a heading that refers to a statement by the president of the Security Council. And if we -- on 25 February 1993. And if we go over to the next page, please, you see at the top of that -- and if you have trouble seeing it, please say and I can [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I see it. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You see at the top of that page the Security Council issuing a statement of deep concern that in spite of its repeated demands, relief efforts continue to be impeded by Serb paramilitary units, especially in the eastern part of the country and the enclaves of Srebrenica and Cerska and Gorazde. And if we can go -- just move down to the bottom of this page. On the 3rd of March, 1993, the president of the Security Council issued another statement and we see that, that the Security Council indicate -- indicates that it was condemning continuing unacceptable military attacks in Eastern Bosnia, condemning the resulting deterioration in the humanitarian situation in the region, and that it was appalled that even as peace talks are continuing, attacks by Serb paramilitary units, including, reportedly, the killings of innocent civilians were continuing in Eastern Bosnia. So, Mr. Davinic, that's the public picture of what was happening in Bosnia at that time - right? - from the words of the Security Council. Fair?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- and -- and you would have known about that, because you're a very senior-level diplomat?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That's your presumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you. Security and disarmament was at the core of your function in peacekeeping. That's what -- you gave a statement to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. But then I would have to educate you the difference between what was happening in -- in that part of the world, in any other parts of the world, and my responsibilities. My responsibilities pertain to international security and disarmament as they relate to international agreements, such as on prohibition of nuclear weapons, on chemical weapons, on ban of conventional armaments, and so on. And thus my responsibilities did not deal with issues pertaining to actual conflicts in any part of the world. Therefore, I had nothing to do with the procedures of the Security Council that pertained to my responsibility as the head of the office for disarmament fairs or the Centre for Disarmament Affairs. And therefore, if I knew anything about what was going on in the Security Council, I knew it as an individual as any other but not in my official capacity. I did not attend the meetings of the Security Council, I did not receive the documents of the Security Council, and it was up to me to get these documents just for the sake of knowing what was happening in the country to which I belonged and where I wanted to go back to after my service in the United Nations. I hope that you understand what I'm saying and that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It does. Did you know about it? Did you know that this was the situation, these were the reports of what was going on in Eastern Bosnia at that time in whatever capacity, Dr. Davinic?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I -- if you wish me, I will repeat it once again. It was not part of my responsibilities and therefore I did not follow it officially. If I follow it privately, maybe I followed, maybe I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, did you or didn't you? Did you know that there was a humanitarian tragedy that was unfolding in Srebrenica in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. The way you ask me, I had to answer, no, I did not, because you're not really listening to what I am saying. And if I may say, you're twisting my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I do not agree Ms. Edgerton ever twisted your words. Her question was whether you knew or not whether such circumstances as referred to in this report existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, if you please. I may answer once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my official capacity, I did not know anything about this, I did not receive documents, I was not aware of that, and it was not part of my responsibilities. In my private capacity as an individual, who was concerned about the future of my country which turned out not to be anymore my country in that size, I may have known or I may have not known. It was long time ago, and over the period of time there were a lot of reports about crimes, about terrible things happening in that part of the world committed by both side, by all sides, as a matter of fact, in this conflict, and I cannot pin-point, and I say that in all honesty with the intention to help this Court, that I cannot confirm with certainty that at that particular point when Mr. Karadzic came to my office I was fully aware of everything that was going on in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when Dr. Karadzic dropped in at your office in March of 1993, whenever he dropped in, you didn't discuss the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina with him?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: He had actually a meeting with the Secretary-General on the 38th floor. My office was on the 36th floor of the building, the UN building. And as I indicated in my statement he had heard from someone from the mission or at that time it was not -- it was actually a mission of Yugoslavia, but suspended from the membership, that there was someone from Belgrade serving in that high position and he expressed a desire to drop by and say hello. So he came to my office with his associates, and as I said I think in my statement I took the initiative of telling him in my private capacity of why the implications in the world of what was going on in the country based on my attendance of various international meetings in which security issues were discussed in general, and some preferences were made to the situation in Bosnia. And my talk with him focussed on the consequences that might actually occur after the end of the war for -- related to alleged war crimes and other crimes committed by warring sides in that conflict, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also in Croatia. And I believe in my statement I said that he listen with great attention, and I was quite surprised that he did not challenge what I was telling him. He listened very carefully. One of his associates - I don't remember his name - I think I mentioned was not particularly interested in listening to what I was saying, but he was. And his comment was basically that this was so because the international community was not properly and fully informed of what's going on and that the international media misled the public opinion throughout the world by presenting the one-sided picture of -- of gruesome crimes and other things which were happening, and he said that that is exactly what he was trying to explain to the Secretary-General, and with these words that he hoped that the situation, that the public opinion would, as a matter of fact, change its view of Serbian action. He departed, and he said that he would like to meet me whenever I had opportunity to visit him and that he would appreciate my views on what -- what was going on with regard to Bosnia and peace efforts that he was involved in. And that was the gist of -- of the meeting which lasted, and I would like to point out once again, to emphasise, that actually I did most of the talking about international ramifications of what was going on and that the way things looked to me -- and they didn't bode well for the leadership of Republika Srpska and that something had to be done, either in terms of reaching peace agreement or changing the perception that the world had about Serbian action there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, looking at what I have just told you about the context and the perception that the world had of Serbian action in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would take Dr. Karadzic's assertion that the world didn't have the a truthful picture of what was happening to mean that he was saying the Security Council's concerns were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I believe that this sounds like your -- your conclusion. Because at that time, as I said, and I will repeat once again, I was not aware of what the Security Council had adopted. And, therefore, his remarks -- I could not challenge his remarks because I didn't have basis to challenge him. He simply said what he said and I didn't have any reason to doubt the sincerity of what he was saying. But I would like to emphasise once again, maybe I did not explain myself clearly, I told him that there was a worldwide perception of gruesome things happening in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina and most of those things were attributed to the Serb side. And I told him that -- I say it once again that either he should bring the truth to the fore, if he could, or that something should be done to stop these things from happening because there might be a very serious consequences for those who would be charged later on with committing these kind of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. I'd like to show you a document that dates from the 12th of March, 1993, and it's in relation to what you mentioned in paragraph 4. You talked about Serbian authorities there. And I'd like to show you P6161. It's some excerpts from the stenographic notes of the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council from 12 March, 1993. And I think if we go to the page 2 in your language, Dr. Davinic, and just stay at the bottom of page 1 in English for the moment. I'd just like to direct you to a reference where Mr. Bulatovic says to the meeting: "We are obliged to understand that we can hardly co-operate with someone who, like the prime minister of the Republika Srpska, advises us to ethnically cleanse Sandzak and kill the Muslims there." And then President Milosevic says: "Who?" And if you flip over to the next page in English, Mr. Bulatovic explains that it's the prime minister of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Lukic, who advises the SDC to do this as soon as possible because Muslims weren't to be trusted. Now you talked about concerns about what was going on in Bosnia. It's clear from this, Dr. Davinic, that in March of 1993 the Serbian authorities actually had serious concerns about the extremist views of some Bosnian Serb leaders supporting ethnic cleansing; right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: If you say so, because I don't know how you relate this to me. I mean, I was UN official. I had nothing to do with the meetings of Supreme Defence Council or whatever it was called in Milosevic's areas, and I had no contacts with them to be informed, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, at paragraph 4 of your statement in the English version that we have, you talked about the concerns of Serbian authorities about the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: If you would allow me just to remind myself. I have to read it. I think that if I may, Your Honour, the sentence is very clear. I was referring to discussions in that conference in Japan at which the situation -- the security situation was discussed worldwide with special references to what was going on in the Balkans, and I said that the perception that it created worldwide - let me see once again - were giving rise to concerns both to the authorities in Serbia and also in Republika Srpska. It is my conclusion based on what I heard, and, as I tried to explain, my impression was that -- concern was so great that eventually the consequences will be followed at one particular point in time when all this is over. My reference to concerns of the authorities is not based on my knowledge that they were concerned. I was suggesting that they should be concerned in view of what was happening and it was widely perceived by the international community and also in the UN that Serbia at that time was helping war efforts in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that based on concerns expressed by the international community, that this was contributing to the war efforts going on in -- in those two former republics of Yugoslavia that they -- the question would be asked and that therefore it was time to consider how to rectify this situation. This is what I was telling Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes -- that amplifies what you said in your statement and actually makes it much clearer, and it allows us to move on to what you said at paragraph 5, 6, and 7, and 8 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In relation to Markale II, there you were talking about some comments from two colleagues, and one of whose name you couldn't remember, and -- your comments related to the integrity of the Markale II investigation. Now, in the summary of your evidence, Dr. Karadzic said you believed that for political reasons, the UN wanted to ensure that the investigation would conclude that the attack came from the Serbs. But that's actually not expressed in your statement at all. So was Dr. Karadzic's summary of your evidence correct? Is that what you believe?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to say what I believed in, or do you want me to explain the factual situation? Because I can tell you what I believed in, but it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like you to -- there seems to be a discrepancies between what Dr. Karadzic understood your evidence to be and read out into the public record and what you said in your statement. So I'd like to clarify what your position was. Is your position simply that you heard from two colleagues in New York some observations about the integrity of the investigation, or is your position that the investigation was specifically targeted against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: In order to respond to your question, if Your Honour would allow me, I have to give you a more detailed explanation as to what actually happened, and then we can draw the conclusion as to what my position is or was at that time, if you would allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to understand, I'm asking you this because of the discrepancy --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- between what Dr. Karadzic said and what you've written in your statement.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat your statement because we've received that evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
