utterances.text: Why don't we see what he wrote in his statement first. Let's find out whether there's a discrepancy at all. Probably paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraphs 6, 7, and 8. So that would be pages 2 and 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could repeat Mr. Karadzic's summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic said that Dr. Davinic believed that for political reasons the United Nations wanted to ensure that the investigation concluded that the attack came from the Serb side. And that's at temporary transcript page 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the crux of the question was, since we -- we could not find the exact passage Mr. Karadzic referred to in your statement, whether it is a consistent summary of your evidence or not. Can you answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer could be found in paragraph 8 of my written statement, which is, I believe, quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of your written statement recounts what you heard from a Greek colleague, who you don't identify, who said that the political reasons had outweighed in the investigation on the ground, which had been given the task of proving the attack came from the Serb side. So that's your position, not the position of your Greek colleague?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: This is the position which I described as the information which I had received from my colleague, who was working, actually, in the Department for Peacekeeping Operations, and, as such, was knowledgeable of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've heard -- the Tribunal has heard, actually, in several proceedings a lot about the investigation of that incident. It's received evidence of showing an extremely broad UN investigation into the shelling, and there wasn't just one but three technical analyses from -- that involved a range of military people from different nations, and that included people with experience in crater analysis and people who were on the scene at the time, and they've heard evidence about their impartiality and their professionalism. And in those -- that investigation included crater analysis, ballistics analysis, acoustics analysis, measurements, photos. So your colleague, whose name you can't remember, is asserting that these people who performed this wide investigation were all in collusion. That's not your position at all, is it, Dr. Davinic?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I have no position on this issue because I was not involved in investigations in -- in that place where this incident had taken place. I did not have access to reports, technical reports of the UN investigating teams or all other teams. What I'm saying here is that a colleague of mine who was very much involved in the work of peacekeeping operations in -- in the Balkans, upon meeting me in passing, did mention this as something that was much on his mind and that he felt that he should tell me this. However, if you would permit me, Your Honour, I think that this -- what I'm saying here must be seen in conjunction with previous paragraphs in which I explain what preceded this statement of colleague of mine that you mention I can't remember his name, because this, as a matter of fact, would make some sense. For some, this would confirm this allegation that the instruction was to give -- to put emphasis on the Serbian side, the responsibility; or some would consider that it was conjunctional kind of statement, private statement, and therefore it has no relevance. If you allow me, Your Honour, and if you don't mind, I will refer back to few paragraphs earlier than paragraph 8, in which I explained that that morning and we met --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, with respect, Mr. Davinic, I don't need you to repeat your testimony in your written evidence.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to confirm, then, you've never seen any part of the technical reports into these investigations that I've just alluded to parts of. You've never seen it. I just want you to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that I have not seen for the very simple reason that it was not within the purview of my responsibility. However, what you're trying to prevent me from saying is that I was privy to political discussions which had the relevance to precisely what you are trying to indicate as casual remark of no relevance to what we are doing here. So you draw your own conclusion, but I'm not happy that you are preventing me from putting things together. Because I can talk only about political aspects of this case. I'm not technical expert. I was minister of disarmament -- of defence but actually not technical expert in weaponry and other things. I'm expert in political issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You weren't privy to anything that was going on, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: In technical terms, no; in political terms, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you actually -- you don't know that on that day, on the 28th of August, 1995, there wasn't just one shell that fell on the centre of Sarajevo. There were five, 120-millimetre mortars that were launched and impacted on the centre of the city between 10.50 in the morning and 11.15 that morning. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, you do know now?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Not now. You never asked me if I knew or I didn't know. You asked me if I was privy to technical reports. I was not privy to technical reports, but I had information how many shells were fired and which exploded, which did not explode, and I think that one that exploded exploded at 11.05 and not 11.15. But it is immaterial; it exploded, one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you know this, that five shells impacted, do you know then that the primary charges on each of those mortars, that sort of core element of those mortars, bore the marks of having been manufactured in Krusik Valjevo in Serbia. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. And it is not relevant to political discussion which took place I was privy to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know that that same marking which -- which showed -- which showed that the primary charge was manufactured in Krusik Valjevo in Serbia was also found on a mortar that exploded on the 18th of June, 1995, in Dobrinja in Sarajevo on a water-line. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: I think it is totally irrelevant to what I am witness to in these proceedings. I can give you some examples where, for instance, American-made shells were used in various conflicted in the world by terrorist organisations, Al-Qaeda, and so on and so forth. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Davinic, that doesn't answer my question --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- did you know it or not?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think that is quite responsive to the question. He should be allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me questions which, in my opinion, are irrelevant to my testimony here. You're asking me technical details and I know what is the purpose of this. I -- I'm -- Your Honour, I'm ready to oblige and ready to clarify, but if the Prosecution is asking me irrelevant questions that we know for sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davinic, whether it is relevant or irrelevant will be monitored and ruled by us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you could answer the question in a simpler manner. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know the designations of the production or manufacturer of these particular shells or weapons that were used, allegedly used -- or, not allegedly, it appears that according to you that they were indeed used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to go on to one other area and it's about your meeting with Dr. Karadzic, the first meeting, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because in your statement, you -- you note that Dr. Karadzic told you at the time of the shelling the entire Bosnian Serb army refused to obey his orders.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: He told me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the eve of the air-strikes, actually it was on the 4th of September, 1995, Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic and Mr. Krajisnik were in telephone contact, and General Mladic recorded those conversations on dictaphone cassettes, and I want to show you a section from a transcript of one of those, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 35038 at page 12. And page 12 is the English language reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, so these three men were in conversation and they were discussing ways to avoid shelling that night. And at the very bottom of this page in English, General Mladic says to Dr. Karadzic: "You see, let me tell you, I cannot but act in keeping with your decisions, your [sic] directives, and in line with my legal authority." So despite what Dr. Karadzic said to you in 1996, at the time General Mladic was telling Karadzic he was subservient. It doesn't look -- this looks like a functioning chain of command, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: It doesn't to me. Since I had experience or have had experience and as minister of defence I know what is the relationship between the minister and chief of general staff and members of General Staff. I am -- would not interpret it that way, but I'm not saying this in order to defend Mr. Karadzic, I'm simply responding to your question which was very explicit, asking me whether this was someone subordinate who the president of -- of -- of -- of the authority or not. To me, it doesn't sound like that, but that's my personal view. You asked for my personal view, not official interpretation of what transpired. Because he also refers here to his legal authority. When my generals referred to their legal authority, that meant don't interfere in what we are doing. And this is not perhaps the time or the place, but I can tell you what problems I had with my generals when we were hunting General Ratko Mladic and I was in charge of these operations when we used foreign aircrafts to chase him in -- in various parts of Serbia, how they responded, and how I had to overrule them by going to even higher top authorities of the country at that time. So, therefore, based on my experience, this legal responsibility of the chief -- of the general -- commander, chief of general staff, gave him a great deal of responsibility. But, please, I'm responding only to your questions. I am not taking sides as to who was responsible, who was not responsible. I'm giving interpretation because you asked me to give you interpretation whether or not this was actually something that is in line with your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you completely discount General Mladic's statement to Dr. Karadzic that he "cannot but act in keeping with your decisions and directives." You completely discount that.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. You ask me whether I -- you asked me for my interpretation. I said that his reference to his legal authority to me means that he has a great deal of freedom to act on his own within that legal authority and nothing beyond this. My interpretation doesn't go beyond this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just going to leave that and ask you one further question, just to follow up on something you've alluded to in your hunt for General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said repeatedly in 2004, particularly, that General Mladic -- you said in statements to the press, you said: General Mladic was not on the territory of this country. You said that.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- and that was the time you were defence minister for Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At that time, we all now know that General Mladic was being moved between different rented apartments in Belgrade. And, Mr. Davinic, he was being moved in military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: The question is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you said to the public in September 2004 that General Mladic was not on the territory of this country, that General Mladic wasn't being protected by the army, that was untrue, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Well, that's your interpretation. And I take offence in your words that it is not true. In other words you're saying I'm lying. I am not. And I will, with your permission, Your Honour, explain why you're wrong and I'm right. You see, General Mladic, according to publicly available documents, was in public view until year 2002. When we adopted Law on Co-operation with the Tribunal, he disappeared. And he disappeared from military facility and it was not known where he was hiding subsequently. Well, later on, we discovered a lot of things but that was at the time when I was no longer defence minister. However, just to prove that I'm right in what I am saying or what I was saying at the time, I will then describe, with your permission, how we hunted General Mladic in September 2004. By the way, I had a meeting with Carla Del Ponte at that time, here in this building, a few days after unsuccessful attempt to apprehend him to discuss further steps. But that's beyond I believe your interest. The interest at that time was that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Davinic, it's correct, isn't it, that he was being moved from place to place in VJ military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: After 2002, I presume it is not. But you interrupted me at very important point which -- which proves that you are wrong. Because, you see, at the time when in 2004, Carla Del Ponte informed American authorities that General Mladic would from Bosnia -- or, rather, Republika Srpska cross into Serbia and meet his family in one of the monasteries on the border with Republika Srpska. And the authorities from Washington through their embassy in Belgrade requested us to permit at her request that their reconnaissance plane --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Davinic --

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I just asked you about the movement of General Mladic from place to place in VJ military vehicles. And you said -- you said that you presumed that that was untrue.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. Again, we have problem in communication, so, therefore, I will be very slow in responding. I said that until 2002 it was publicly known that he was in Belgrade, attending football matches, attending concerts, going to wedding parties, and so on, and then after the adoption of the Law on Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal, he disappeared. What happened after that was not known to me while I was minister of defence. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I think then you finally came to the answer of the question.

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No. I would ask the Court to add one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you make it -- so what is your question? What is your answer to the question of Ms. Edgerton, whether Mr. Mladic was being moved in Belgrade on VJ vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I don't know. I know, however, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you didn't know at that time. Do you now know that it was the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not follow this after his arrest. However, I know that he was supposed to come from Bosnia to Serbia in September 2004. That I know for sure because that was discussed with Carla Del Ponte. And it was unsuccessful attempt to apprehend him, although we did everything possible, together with American reconnaissance plane, and special forces which were borrowed from UNPROFOR. So, my point is that, at that time in September 2004, he was supposed to come from Bosnia to Serbia. I'm not defending, Your Honour, Mladic. Or I'm not actually speaking on his behalf. I, in all honesty, don't know what is the purpose of questioning me on General Mladic because I'm here as witness to say what I discussed with Dr. Karadzic. Nevertheless, I'm very pleased to be able to explain my -- my knowledge of what was going on with regard to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Davinic, on page 79, there was some insistence on the question concerning your meeting with me while you knew I -- that I was a fugitive in the first half or the second half of 1996. Did you have any knowledge about any kind of agreement that I may have had that I would not be tried?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, no. Absolutely not as a result of anything to do with the cross-examination. I normally don't interrupt Dr. Karadzic, but the witness is speaking rather quickly, and I just wanted this to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think this arises from the line of cross-examination. You should have dealt with it in your direct examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I believe there was a dose of reprimand in the cross-examination in that question concerning Mr. Davinic meeting with me while knowing that I was a fugitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't see there was a reprimand there. So please move onto another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Davinic, you were shown on page 83 an UN document, describing the conduct of Serbian paramilitaries. Did you understand what my attitude was towards paramilitaries and was it made known to the UN?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know your -- your attitude towards paramilitary forces. My impression is that you had nothing to do with that and that is paramilitary forces were under direct guidance, control of different authorities. It was widely believed that some of them were controlled by Serbia, and by Milosevic, and that some of them were just rogue sections of the military that were involved in robbery and crimes and other things on their own, and I didn't hear anyone at that time or later attributing or connecting you with this. I say this based on my knowledge. I'm not saying that it was true or not true. Simply, I didn't have any knowledge of your connection with these paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What, Mr. Davinic, did you have in mind when you said a group controlled by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my knowledge. It was widely perceived by the international community, and you could read in all sort of media reports that some of those forces were directed and financed by Milosevic and his State Security Service. So this is -- this is public knowledge which is not -- I was not privy to any secret documents or any discussions with anyone that might have disclosed to me something that was not known publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the minutes here do not reflect exactly what I actually said here. It says 35, 45, whatever it is, I do not have a normal of your connection with this -- I did not have any information of your connection -- or knowledge. I would say I said I did not have any knowledge of your connection with these paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just want to show you one letter, D1933 in e-court, please. Dr. Davinic, this is a letter addressed to the UN Secretary-General. Does it define my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Again -- and I sat through the last session where Dr. Karadzic did the same thing. This is re-direct examination. He can ask the question without showing the witness the document first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 102, line 11. I did cite a foundation. A document of the UN was shown dealing with the activities of the paramilitaries that were certainly connected in me. It was just shown to Dr. Davinic to ask him whether these paramilitaries that are said to be somehow involved with me were doing such and such things. And I'm asking Dr. Davinic how that would be viewed by the United Nations, if they had received this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that witness already answered he didn't know about your position towards paramilitaries, would there be any further point asking further questions in relation to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I've grown rusty in my legal skills over the break, but I'll get the hang of it soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Davinic, if the Chamber will not allow it -- but with their leave, I would like you to answer on these letters. Was it an isolated opinion of that friend of yours from the United Nations concerning the political wishes to assign blame for Markale 1995?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: No, it was not, actually. It was a widespread belief. And many people in the corridors and in the delegates' lounge were talking about that, especially a few months later when NATO bombing started and when Serbian forces were actually pushed back from the siege of Sarajevo and when the peace process actually got under way. Many people were saying -- but, again, I'm just conveying what I heard in the corridors that that was a very fortunate occurrence in the Markale place which led then to decisive actions by -- by the NATO forces to stop actually the fighting and then to initiate the peace process, which resulted in the Dayton and Paris Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P150 briefly. P150.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page. We need just the English. Oh, there is a translation. Next page, please. Could we zoom in on number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Davinic, I believe you'll be able to make out this handwriting, or I will try, if you wish: [In English] "The investigating team tried very hard to prove that the attack came from the Serb side due to the normal use of heavy mortars that is likely, but there is a hard -- no hard proof on this fact," or something like that. [Interpretation] Is this consistent with what you heard at the headquarters of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before there is an answer on this, I just want to make the point that Dr. Karadzic is being a bit disingenuous with this document. There is evidence, the evidence is from the author of this document who's testified here that the reference to the investigation team does not refer to the UN investigation team. The evidence -- and it's Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, and I will be able to find the reference in his evidence very briefly. But the evidence from Lieutenant-Colonel Konings is that this reference to the investigation team refers to the local team on the ground, not his team which conducted their work impartially and with integrity. So if Dr. Karadzic is going to ask the question, I think it's appropriate for him not to be disingenuous and say what the document really is and take the surrounding evidence into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did Mr. Karadzic refer to this as being the UN investigating team?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, he has not specifically, Your Honour. He says this is a report by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. And then he referred immediately to point number 3 without explaining what that remark referred to. Hence my point that Dr. Karadzic is being somewhat disingenuous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the intervention, I believe that witness is now able to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I cannot comment on whether or not this referred to the UN report or any investigation carried out by somebody else. I can only comment that that morning at the meeting with the under-secretary general for political affairs, we got information that an attack had occurred earlier this morning and that the problem with this was two-fold. It created shock at the UN for two reasons. One was humanitarian because a large number of casualties occurred. Over 40 dead and twice as many injured. And that was a civilian target and that created lot of concern. The other concern expressed at that meeting related to a political aspect of this because the report - and maybe this, what I will say, has some -- maybe it has some reference to what Dr. Karadzic referred to now - did not indicate prima facie that one side could be -- that -- that -- that this shelling could be attributed to one side, the Serbian side. The first report was inconclusive in terms of who could have committed this crime. And, therefore, it could be one or the other side. And then serious concerns were expressed as to who could have done it because there was already rather well-established worldwide opinion that most of these things were done by the Serbian side, and if this could be proven with further investigation in the field, this would fit into the general perception. However, since this first report did not -- was not able to establish beyond shadow of a doubt that one side was clearly responsible and that it allowed that either side could have committed this particular attack, the instruction was issued to carry out investigation to the fullest possible extent and as -- as neutrally as possible because if -- and this is the part which is rather important. Because if the investigation were to prove that the other side may have done this, it would have serious political ramifications throughout the world because this other side was perceived for years as the victim in this war. Therefore, the instruction from the UN came, very strict instruction, that every effort must be done to establish the truth beyond shadow of a doubt. Then the second report -- or the report that came both oral and later written -- I'm not privy to the written directly. I only heard. That this reporting indicated possibility of the shell coming from either side, but in view of everything else and maybe the evidence that the Prosecution pointed to, that it is more likely that it came from the Serbian side. And it is in this context that my Greek colleague - that the Prosecution referred to as unknown; I could not remember the name - told me in passing that political considerations prevailed in giving credence more to the possibility that it was perpetrated by the Serbian side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just explain something. I just asked whether what Dr. Davinic heard from this Greek was just this one sole occasion or whether there were more things said to that effect. Let's see what General Janvier wrote about that. P906, please, could we take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just wanted to let you know the Chamber must rise five to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We are done, Excellency. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said, Dr. Davinic, that you hadn't seen the report but that you did here what was being said that. Now I'm going read this sentence to you. Line 7 or 8: "[In English] The definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult as it is impossible to determine the level of charged -- charge used to fire the projectile." [Interpretation] Does this correspond to what you had heard about the reports of the UN? Do you know who General Janvier was?

utterances.speaker: PRVOSLAV DAVINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I know, certainly, who the general was. And, once again, let me make it absolutely clear. This was talk of the day. Everybody was talking in the UN corridors and in the conference hall and in the delegates' lounge about this, so it was kind of a public secret. I'm saying "public secret." Let me define what I mean. That the issue in the opinion of those -- and I'm just conveying what I had heard. This is not my opinion. I'm just saying what I had heard. That this whole incident, tragic incident, was not investigated to the fullest. And that it -- the -- the -- the conclusion that it is most likely -- or more likely that the Serbian side perpetrated this crime came in rather handy for the political process that took place subsequent to this particular incident. And that's what people were talking in the corridors. I did not discuss with them officially. I didn't ask them for their opinion. I simply overheard them talking in the cafeteria, in delegates' lounge having cup of coffee, or in some other informal circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having testified, Dr. Davinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution, and Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed, on behalf of the Chamber, the Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was pleasure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hearing is adjourned. We'll continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
